summary: Defines how to carry an MPLS label stack and its payload over L2TPv3 data encapsulation. This lets applications that usually need an MPLS core run over a plain IP network.

eli5.summary: MPLS normally needs special roads. This puts MPLS traffic inside L2TPv3 tunnels so it can travel over ordinary IP networks that lack those roads.

questions: how to carry mpls over ip
subtitle: How to carry MPLS label stacks inside L2TPv3 so MPLS applications can run over a plain IP network.

tldr.problem: Some applications normally need an MPLS-enabled core network, but the path between two routers may be only plain IP.
tldr.mechanism: The MPLS label stack and its payload are carried unchanged after the IP and L2TPv3 headers. The L2TPv3 Session ID is required, and an optional random Cookie helps validate the packet source.
tldr.outcome: MPLS can cross an IP network with more spoofing protection than plain IP or GRE, at less cost than IPsec.

today: RFC 4817 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: MPLS Inside L2TPv3
sections.content:
RFC 4817 defines how to encapsulate an MPLS label stack and its payload inside the tunnel payload of the Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol, Version 3 (L2TPv3). L2TPv3 tunnels a variety of payload types over IP networks. This lets an application that traditionally requires an MPLS-enabled core use L2TPv3 over an IP network instead.

The document only describes encapsulation. It does not cover all the MPLS-based applications that could run over L2TPv3. It also discusses other ways to carry MPLS over IP, namely IP, GRE and IPsec, in an applicability section.
sections.eli5: This note says how to wrap MPLS packets inside another kind of tunnel so they can travel over normal internet-style networks.

sections.title: The Encapsulation
sections.content:
The MPLS label stack and payload are carried in their entirety after the IP header (IPv4 or IPv6) and the L2TPv3 header. The layering is IP, then L2TPv3, then the MPLS label stack, then the MPLS payload.

The Session ID MUST be present. It is a 32-bit identifier chosen locally as a lookup key for the context of an L2TP session, which includes whether a Cookie is present, its value, and what kind of encapsulation follows. The Cookie MAY be present. It is a variable-length value of at most 64 bits that MUST be cryptographically random and MUST NOT be the same as a recently used value for a given Session ID. It guards against misdirected stray packets, a corrupted Session ID, and some malicious packet insertion.

The L2TPv3 L2-Specific Sublayer MAY be present but is generally not. Fragmentation, MTU, TTL, EXP and DSCP handling follow the common procedures in Section 5 of RFC 4023. The Session ID and Cookie can be configured manually or distributed by a signaling protocol, which this RFC leaves out of scope.
sections.eli5: The MPLS packet goes in a box labeled with a ticket number (Session ID) and, if wanted, a secret password (Cookie). The box then rides in an ordinary IP envelope.

sections.title: When to Prefer It
sections.content:
Three methods carry MPLS over IP: RFC 4023 (IP or GRE), a PE-PE IPsec architecture, and this one. The RFC argues that border routers find it simpler to refuse MPLS packets outright than to filter certain MPLS packets carried in IP or GRE, so IP or GRE raise the chance that an MPLS label-spoofing attack succeeds. Checking the L2TPv3 Cookie acts like an access list on a header value that is very hard to spoof.

MPLS over L2TPv3 may be advantageous when two routers are already adjacent over an L2TPv3 tunnel for another reason, when hardware can process L2TPv3 faster, or when spoofing and insertion are a worry. In summary, it offers a balance between the limited protection of RFC 4023 and the greater security, and the extra overhead, of the IPsec approach.
sections.eli5: There are several ways to send MPLS over ordinary networks. This one adds a secret code check, which is safer than the simplest ways and lighter than full encryption.

sections.title: Congestion
sections.content:
When an MPLS/L2TPv3 flow carries IP-based traffic, the aggregate is assumed to be TCP friendly because the payload traffic has its own congestion control, so no extra action is needed.

When it carries payload that is not known to be TCP friendly across an unprovisioned path that could become congested, the application MUST add mechanisms to reduce offered load during congestion. The flow should not exceed the average bandwidth a TCP flow would get on the same path. The RFC says the comparison is an order-of-magnitude one, and points to RFC 3448 as one method. It is not acceptable to deploy such an application on the best-effort Internet if it consumes bandwidth arbitrarily.
sections.eli5: If the traffic is not polite about sharing the road, the sender has to slow down when the road gets crowded, just like a regular TCP connection would.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names three concerns when carrying MPLS-labeled traffic between PEs over IP tunnels: a third party inserting packets, viewing the stream, or altering packets. Operators can use access lists, authentication, encryption and context validation, and should weigh the cost of each.

Without IPsec, address filtering at domain boundaries only works well within a single administrative domain. If only source address filtering is done, the decapsulator MUST effectively validate the IP source address. The Cookie is not encryption, but if it is a sufficiently random 64-bit value kept secret from an off-path attacker, it is a simple, effective source check that resists brute-force spoofing.

To secure the tunnel with IPsec, transport mode SHOULD be used, and authentication and integrity MUST be provided. Implementations MUST support ESP with null encryption, and MAY support ESP with encryption if confidentiality is needed. Manual keying MUST be supported, and if automatic keying is implemented, IKE in main mode with preshared keys MUST be supported. A tunnel tail MUST discard an MPLS packet without IPsec encapsulation whose top label is in the set it distributed to IPsec-secured tunnel heads.
sections.eli5: The secret code on the box stops strangers from slipping fake boxes into the delivery line. For stronger protection, the whole truck can also be locked with IPsec.
